title: The big lookout
hookLine: year one is done; ahead lie the ranges: the daily banis, the long story, the ways of the Guru, the Granth itself

lines: THE VALLEY BEHIND, SMALL AND GOLDEN.
cards: Near the top of a long hike, tired legs earn a stop. A hiker turns around, and there it is: the whole valley walked through, small and golden below. Then the other way: more mountains, bigger ones, blue in the distance.
Two thoughts can arrive at once: I made it, and look how much more there is. This is that spot, the last day of year one.

teach.h: SIKH: A LEARNER WHO KEEPS LEARNING.
teach.b: Start with the word Sikh. It's usually traced to an old Indian word for a student, a disciple, a learner. Sikhs often put it simply: a Sikh is someone who keeps learning from the Guru, not someone who finishes.
So a year doesn't end with a diploma; it ends at a lookout. Turn around first.

teach.h: THE VALLEY: WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES, DEPTHS.
teach.b: You began with first words: seva, Waheguru, Ik Onkar, langar, sangat. Then the stories: ten Gurus, one light. Then the practices: kirtan, simran, Nitnem, a visit to the gurdwara.

Then the Japji, pauri by pauri, all thirty-eight and the saloks. Then the depths: the Granth's great themes, Kabir and Farid, the rehat, the history, and the grief of 1984 carried carefully. That's the valley.

teach.h: THE RANGES: BANIS, STORY, WAYS, GRANTH.
teach.b: Four ranges. First, the daily banis: Jaap Sahib tomorrow, then Anand Sahib, Rehras, Kirtan Sohila, Sukhmani, the prayers many Sikhs say morning and evening. Then Sikh history, told slowly, century by century.
Then the ways of the Guru, lived day to day. And then the Granth itself, fourteen hundred thirty pages, the Guru Sikhs bow to. Daunting?

Sikhs have a phrase for the spirit to meet it with, from day seventeen: chardi kala. Rising spirits, an unbeaten, upward-facing mind. It sits in the Ardas's last line, right beside yesterday's good of all.
Chardi kala isn't pretending things are easy. The Sikh story has plenty of hard days, and this year's path passed through some of them.

teach.h: CHARDI KALA: FACE FORWARD, IN GOOD HEART.
teach.b: It's facing forward anyway, in good heart, because the road is long and the company is good.
That's the lookout: grateful behind, awake ahead.

how: Sikhs often describe themselves as lifelong learners of the Guru, and the Ardas said at the close of gurdwara gatherings ends by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, and the good of all.

o: rising spirits, facing forward in good heart
a victory cry shouted before a battle
keeping a brave face and hiding your grief

games.q: the big lookout — tap the pairs.

s: the word Sikh means someone who has finished learning
it is usually traced to an old word for a student or disciple: a Sikh keeps learning from the Guru.
chardi kala means pretending everything is fine
it's facing forward in good heart even on hard days, not denying them.
chardi kala appears in the last line of the Ardas
it sits beside the request for the good of all, sarbat da bhala.

games.q: you've climbed a whole year of the path and reached the lookout. what does the word Sikh suggest comes next?
o: stop here: the learning is complete.
keep walking: a Sikh is a learner for life.
go back to the bottom and start over.
games.why: the word Sikh is usually traced to a word for a learner or disciple. the lookout isn't the end of the road; ahead lie the daily banis, the long story, the ways of the Guru and the Granth itself.

practice: Find a window and let your eyes go as far as they can: a rooftop, a tree, a strip of sky.
Breathe slowly and think back over one word, one story, one practice that stayed with you this year; then let your gaze go to the edge of what you can see, and notice there is more out there.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru under your breath, the Sikh word of wonder from camp one; if not, simply stay with what you see.

wordCard.voice: Chardi kala. Rising spirits, an unbeaten, upward-facing mind — the spirit to meet the ranges ahead, the banis and the Granth, at the top of year one.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: chardi kala, rising spirits; the mood Sikhs meet the road ahead with, named in the Ardas's last line.

carryVoice: Your line: wow. For a sky, a kindness, a sentence that lands. Year one, done.

sources.ref: Ardas, closing line (chardi kala and sarbat da bhala)
sources.work: Ardas, as given in the Sikh Rehat Maryada (SGPC)
